title: US financial conditions shape firm insurance and worker labor-income risk
source_unit: NBER Working Paper 35781, Risk Premia, Firm Insurance, and Endogenous Labor Income Risk

observations.period: Working paper issued September 2026; US administrative data and aggregate financial conditions

denominator.unit: US administrative worker and firm observations; exact sample count not disclosed in the NBER abstract

risk_premia_and_firm_insurance.unit: firm insurance against idiosyncratic shocks erodes when risk premia rise

firm_shock_earnings_pass_through.unit: pass-through of firm shocks to earnings rises in bad times

lower_paid_workers_near_separation.unit: the bad-times increase in earnings pass-through is especially strong for lower-paid workers near the separation margin

recession_contingent_transfers.unit: model implies large welfare gains from recession-contingent transfers

observations.method: Directed-search model with dynamic wage contracts and two-sided limited commitment, combined with US administrative data on worker earnings and firm shocks.
observations.uncertainty: The NBER abstract does not disclose sample counts, effect sizes, exposure windows, or the full identification strategy. The paper is a working paper and combines model results with administrative evidence; earnings risk is not the same as realized household welfare or completed job loss.
observations.subgroup: Lower-paid workers near the separation margin, workers exposed to firm-specific shocks, and firms facing different aggregate risk premia.
observations.counterinterpretation: Bad times may change firm selection, industry composition, hours, outside options, or worker sorting in ways that affect pass-through; modeled welfare gains from transfers depend on the contract, search, discounting, and limited-commitment assumptions.

related_sources.claim: US product-market creative destruction and asymmetric incumbent-worker earnings/job-destruction risk.
US sticky wage norms and real-wage losses during 2021–2024.
US employed workers demand a compensating pay increase for additional unemployment risk in a new job; the job-mobility model supplies a separate insurance-to-mobility comparator.

boundary: This record adds a US financial-conditions-to-firm-insurance-to-worker-risk mechanism. It does not disclose the abstract's omitted effect sizes or sample count, establish a named firm or sector outcome, measure household consumption or political response, or show that recession-contingent transfers were implemented and effective.
